lessons.title: Understanding Document Object Model (DOM) Architecture
lessons.description: The DOM is a tree-shaped representation of your HTML that JavaScript can read and manipulate.

sections.heading: What is the DOM?
paragraphs: When the browser loads an HTML file, it converts every tag into a JavaScript object arranged in a tree. That tree is the Document Object Model (DOM) — your JavaScript's live view of the page.
list: Every HTML element becomes a node object in the tree
The document node sits at the root — the entry point to everything
Parent-child relationships mirror your HTML nesting
You can read, create, modify or remove any node at any time

sections.heading: Why the DOM matters
paragraphs: Without the DOM, JavaScript would have no way to interact with the page. The DOM bridges your code and the visual elements the user sees. Every button click handler, every dynamic text update, every animation triggers through DOM manipulation.

codeExamples.heading: Exploring the DOM in the console
explanation: document is the root — the entire page lives inside it.
head and body are direct shortcuts to those sections.

codeExamples.heading: Traversing the tree
codeExamples.code:
let list = document.querySelector("ul");

console.log(list.parentElement);   // the <ul>'s parent
console.log(list.children);         // all direct child <li>s
console.log(list.firstElementChild); // first <li>
console.log(list.lastElementChild);  // last <li>
explanation: firstElementChild and lastElementChild grab the first and last children.
These properties work in all directions — you can walk the tree freely.

practice.task: Open any web page, open the console, and use document.body.children to see what elements sit directly inside the body. Then try document.body.children[0] to access the first one.
hints: Press F12 to open DevTools, then click the Console tab.
Try document.body.children[0].tagName to see the tag name.

keyTakeaways: The DOM is a tree of JavaScript objects representing your HTML elements.
document is the root — everything else is accessed through it.
You can traverse the tree with parent, child and sibling properties.
JavaScript can read, modify, create or delete any node in the DOM.
lessons.challenge: Write code that finds the first <p> on a page, then logs its parent element's tag name and its own text content.

lessons.title: Selecting Elements with querySelector & querySelectorAll
lessons.description: Use CSS-style selectors to find one or many elements on the page with querySelector and querySelectorAll.

sections.heading: querySelector — find one element
paragraphs: document.querySelector(selector) returns the first element that matches a CSS selector. If nothing matches, it returns null. This is the most flexible and modern way to grab elements.
list: Pass any CSS selector: tag names, classes, IDs, attributes, combinators
Returns a single Element or null
Searches the entire document — or call it on a specific element to search within it

sections.heading: querySelectorAll — find all matches
paragraphs: document.querySelectorAll(selector) returns all matching elements as a static NodeList. Unlike HTMLCollections, NodeLists are snapshots — they won't change if the DOM changes after selection.
list: Use .forEach() or convert with [...nodeList] for array methods
A NodeList is a snapshot — adding/removing elements later doesn't affect it

codeExamples.heading: Selecting by ID, class and tag
explanation: Use #id for ID selectors, .class for class selectors.
The selector syntax is identical to what you'd write in CSS.
Only the first match is returned — even if multiple elements match.

codeExamples.heading: Scoping and querying all matches
explanation: Calling querySelector on an element scopes the search to its descendants.
querySelectorAll gives you a NodeList with all matches.
NodeList supports .forEach() — no conversion needed for simple loops.

practice.task: Select all <li> elements on a page using querySelectorAll, then use forEach to log each one's text content to the console.
hints: Inside forEach, use li.textContent to get the text.

keyTakeaways: querySelector() returns the first matching element using CSS selectors.
querySelectorAll() returns all matches as a static NodeList.
You can scope queries by calling these methods on a specific element.
NodeList supports .forEach() but not .map() directly — spread to convert if needed.
lessons.challenge: Write a function that finds all elements with the class .highlight and changes their background color to yellow using .style.backgroundColor.

lessons.title: Legacy Selectors: getElementById, getElementsByClassName
lessons.description: Older selector methods still appear in codebases — understand how they differ from querySelector.

sections.heading: Legacy methods
paragraphs: Before querySelector existed, developers used these methods to find elements. They still work and you'll encounter them in older code and tutorials.
list: getElementById("id") — returns a single element by its ID
getElementsByName("name") — returns elements by their name attribute

codeExamples.heading: Legacy selector examples
explanation: getElementById is the fastest method — browsers optimize ID lookups.
getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection that updates when the DOM changes.
HTMLCollection is not an array — use [...collection] to convert for map/filter.

practice.task: Use getElementById to select an element with a specific ID, then use getElementsByClassName to get all elements with a class name and log the count.
hints: You need an HTML page with at least one element that has an ID and several elements with the same class.

keyTakeaways: getElementById is the fastest legacy method — one element by ID.
Prefer querySelector and querySelectorAll for new code — they're more flexible and return stable NodeLists.
lessons.challenge: Replace all getElementById calls in a small HTML page with equivalent querySelector("#id") calls. Verify the behavior is identical.

lessons.title: Static NodeLists vs Live HTMLCollections
lessons.description: Understand the difference between static and live element collections and why it matters.

sections.heading: Live vs static collections
paragraphs: Some DOM methods return collections that update automatically when the DOM changes (live), while others return snapshots (static). This difference causes surprising bugs if you don't understand it.
list: Live HTMLCollection — updates automatically when elements are added or removed
Static NodeList — a snapshot that doesn't change after creation

codeExamples.heading: Live HTMLCollection behavior
explanation: The live HTMLCollection automatically picks up the newly added .item element.
The static NodeList is a snapshot from the moment of selection — it stays at 3.
Live collections are convenient but can cause surprises in loops if elements change during iteration.

practice.task: Create a page with 3 .item elements. Select them with both getElementsByClassName and querySelectorAll. Add a 4th item dynamically and log both collection lengths to see the difference.
hints: Use document.createElement("li") to create a new element.

keyTakeaways: Live HTMLCollections update automatically when the DOM changes.
Static NodeLists are snapshots that don't change.
Prefer querySelectorAll for predictable behavior — static snapshots avoid loop surprises.
If you need an array from a NodeList, use Array.from() or the spread operator [...nodeList].
lessons.challenge: Write a loop that removes all .item elements one by one. Test with a live collection vs a static collection and explain the different behavior.
